title: Playing in Kid Ory's band: style, Sheik of Araby, Mack the Knife
summary: Smith recalls following Ory's band in college, then playing trumpet in it on weekends; describes Ory's ensemble style, opener and favorite tunes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Some people like that. Let's talk about Kid Ory. Kid Ory, to me, now we're premising this on the fact that I did play in his band on his pickup gigs and on weekends during the period of about 1958 through 1960. Maybe there was some in 57. I don't know. I recall the George Lewis band at that time, though, in San Francisco. But my early recollections were Ory on Records, of course, those wonderful crescents that came out of Los Angeles, swinging things with Mutt Carey and Bud Scott, and then as I got in college, I used to follow the Ory band. I think nothing of driving 40, 50 miles to catch him at some remote beach resort, playing in some remote ballroom that had the stench of faded gardenias still in it. And I'd hear great people like Bud Scott in his day, and he was a charming mountain of a man who really played. And the band swung, and it was very cohesive, very enjoyable. I remember Buster Wilson, the piano player, doing things like River of the Roses, these wonderful old pop tunes that they would just swing in a very, what I felt was a very polished and wonderful New Orleans style. And then fortunes took me all around, and as I got back to San Francisco, the magic of circumstance brought me in touch with Ory, and he needed a trumpet player, and I was playing a little trumpet at that time. I certainly had my ears hanging out and was listening to his style well enough that I could just step right in and play pretty well. I understood the ensemble playing. I never considered myself a virtuoso soloist. In fact, nobody in Ory's band really specialized in that kind of thing. It was a good, cohesive ensemble band. And I think he was properly named Kidd, if I understand the traditions of that nomenclature. He was a bit of a dude, and he always had a little flash to him, snappy dresser, and he certainly did respond to a crowd, and they responded to him. And he was a strong, strong character. He, as a musician, he had certain little patterns built in. The opener every night was Sheik of Araby. We just automatically, without saying a word, we'd just get up on the stand, and his foot was, you know, he laid with his foot. You know, he'd stomp two times, and we were playing the Sheik of Araby. He'd play the lead. That would loosen him up, and the clarinet and I would be playing the little badadadadadud riffs in the back kind of thing. And by the time the last chorus was going, all the blood was flowing to the lips, and we were ready to play just about anything. And he played a pretty good variety of the things that he's known for on his records. Did he? He liked to play, because Louis had had such a good success with it, he liked to play that song, and this is Ori's words, Max the Knife. Loved to play Max the Knife.
